title: How Stem Cells Keep a Tissue New

scenes.visual: Title card: How Stem Cells Keep a Tissue New.

scenes.tts: The lining of a mouse's small intestine is replaced every few days. Yet the animal keeps it for life. Stem cells make that possible. They sit at the bottom of pockets called crypts, and they do two jobs at once. They keep making every specialized cell of the lining. And they keep up their own numbers. Those two jobs, tested over time, are what make a cell a stem cell.
scenes.visual: A crypt outline. Grey cells stream up the villus and are shed at the tip. Gold stem cells sit at the base. Two labelled arrows leave one gold cell: 'makes specialized cells' going up, and 'makes more stem cells' looping back to the base.

scenes.tts: How would you prove which cells do it? Expressing a gene tells you nothing about fate. So scientists trace cells instead. A pulse of the drug tamoxifen puts a permanent mark in L G R five cells at the crypt base. Every daughter inherits that mark. Over sixty days, the label filled ribbons of epithelium holding every kind of epithelial cell. That shows multipotency within the gut. It does not show pluripotency.
scenes.visual: One base cell turns green when tamoxifen arrives. A green ribbon rises among unlabelled cells over a 60-day bar, with icons for absorptive, goblet, enteroendocrine and Paneth cells. Chips read 'multipotent within the gut' and a crossed-out 'pluripotent'.

scenes.tts: How does the pool stay the same size? These stem cells divide about once a day, and most divisions are symmetric. Daughters stay or leave by chance. Some clones take over a crypt, while others vanish. The population keeps the balance, not each division.
scenes.visual: A crypt base with stem cells in four colours. Cells are replaced at random by copies of neighbours until the base is one colour. A once-a-day clock in the corner.

scenes.tts: What tells a daughter to stay or to leave? Its neighbours, called the niche. At the crypt base, Wint signals keep cells as stem cells. Higher up, B M P signals push them to specialize. Paneth cells help stem cells grow in a dish. But in the living gut, stem cells survived without them, and Wint from cells beneath the lining was needed. The niche has more than one source.
scenes.visual: The crypt with two opposing colour gradients: Wnt strongest at the base, BMP strongest up the villus. Paneth cells and flat stromal telocytes beneath the epithelium both glow as sources. A Paneth cell is removed and the stem cells stay; telocyte Wnt is switched off and proliferation drops.

scenes.tts: Fates are less fixed than that picture suggests. When the L G R five stem cells were killed, the crypt still recovered. Progenitor cells, on their way to becoming absorptive or secretory cells, went back and rebuilt the stem pool. That is an injury result. It does not mean mature cells act as stem cells every day.
scenes.visual: The gold stem cells blink out. Progenitor cells a little way up the crypt turn back down an arrow labelled 'back to stem state' and refill the base. A small tag reads 'after injury only'.

scenes.tts: How far back can a specialized cell go? In nineteen sixty-two, John Gurdon put a nucleus from a tadpole's gut cell into a frog egg without its own nucleus. A small fraction became normal tadpoles. In two thousand six, Shinya Yamanaka's lab used four transcription factors to turn mouse fibroblasts into pluripotent cells. Specialized cells can be reset. Pluripotent is not totipotent, and passing these tests is not the same as being safe in patients.
scenes.visual: Left: a nucleus pipetted into an egg, with most eggs failing and one tadpole swimming. Right: four factor icons enter a fibroblast, which rounds into a pluripotent cell beside three germ-layer icons. Chips read 'not totipotent' and 'not proof of safety'.
